name: Glutathione
used_for: A naturally occurring tripeptide antioxidant (glutamate, cysteine, glycine) made in the body. It is sold as oral and liposomal supplements and offered in clinics as intravenous or injectable therapy, often for skin lightening or general wellness. Small trials show oral glutathione raises blood glutathione and some immune markers, and evidence for skin lightening is limited. Per a 2015 FDA consumer alert reported by Healio, the FDA has not approved any injectable drug for skin lightening, and secondary sources describe FDA concern about injectables compounded from dietary-grade powder.

entries.text: In a 2015 six-month randomized trial, oral glutathione 250 mg/day or 1,000 mg/day was given, with blood glutathione rising at both doses.
In a 2018 one-month pilot study, oral liposomal glutathione 500 mg/day or 1,000 mg/day was given.
In a 2026 crossover pilot, single oral doses of standard glutathione 500 mg and micellar glutathione 300 mg were compared, followed by 30 days of micellar glutathione 600 mg/day.

internet_entries.text: A ScienceInsights explainer says most studies of oral glutathione for skin use daily doses between 250 and 1,000 mg, and that a trial of intravenous glutathione used 1,200 mg twice weekly for six weeks.
internet_entries.population: Studies as described by the source, not a population the source tested itself

administration_guidance.text: A ScienceInsights explainer says oral glutathione is limited by digestive breakdown and takes 6 to 12 weeks for reported effects, topical forms are used for dark spots, and IV gives the highest blood levels but carries the greatest risks.
administration_guidance.label: internet

administration_guidance.text: A crossover trial of oral glutathione formulations in 14 healthy adults reported that a micellar formulation produced higher blood glutathione exposure than standard oral glutathione at the doses tested.
administration_guidance.label: research

side_effects.text: A ScienceInsights explainer says serious reactions concentrate in injectable forms, including severe allergic reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and anaphylaxis, and that IV glutathione with high-dose vitamin C raises kidney stone risk.
side_effects.label: internet

side_effects.text: A dermatology clinic blog lists mild effects of injectable glutathione as nausea, headache and injection-site pain, and serious effects as liver injury, endotoxin-contamination shock-like reactions and anaphylaxis.
side_effects.label: internet

side_effects.text: A Healio report says the FDA stated it has not approved any injectable drug for skin whitening, and that products often containing glutathione are unapproved new drugs with unverifiable contents.
side_effects.label: internet

internet_claims.claim: ScienceInsights says in trials only 37.5% of IV glutathione recipients reported lighter skin vs 18.7% with placebo, with effects described as temporary.
Healio reports the FDA warned that injectable skin-lightening products, often containing glutathione, are unapproved and risk injecting an unknown substance.

research.summary: Six-month randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of oral glutathione in 54 non-smoking adults.
research.finding: Blood glutathione levels rose dose- and time-dependently and returned to baseline after washout; oxidative stress markers fell and natural killer cell activity increased at the higher level.

research.summary: One-month pilot study of oral liposomal glutathione in 12 healthy adults.
research.finding: Raised glutathione in blood compartments and improved oxidative stress and immune function markers; small pilot without placebo group.

research.summary: Randomized crossover pilot in 14 healthy adults comparing standard, liposomal and micellar oral glutathione, plus a 30-day safety follow-up.
research.finding: The micellar formulation gave higher baseline-adjusted glutathione exposure than standard glutathione; tolerability was assessed over 30 days.

research.summary: Double-blind randomized trial in 46 participants of topical and oral glutathione for skin whitening over 8 weeks.
research.finding: Combined topical and oral glutathione lowered the melanin index vs placebo; small trial of oral and topical, not injected, glutathione.

research.summary: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of inhaled glutathione (646 mg in 4 ml by nebulizer every 12 hours for 6 months) in 153 people aged 8 and older with cystic fibrosis. Griese et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med.
research.finding: Lung function (FEV1) did not differ from placebo over 6 months; exacerbations and quality of life were not better. Glutathione reached the airways, but markers of oxidative stress did not fall. Adverse events were similar to placebo.

research.summary: Single-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of inhaled glutathione twice daily for 12 months in 54 adults and 51 children with cystic fibrosis. Calabrese et al., J Cyst Fibros.
research.finding: The preset goal of a 15% improvement in FEV1 was not met. Only people with moderate lung disease showed small FEV1 gains at 3, 6 and 9 months. The treatment was well tolerated.

research.summary: Randomized, double-blind, crossover, placebo-controlled study of nebulized glutathione (600 mg in 4 ml saline over 25 minutes) in 8 people with mild asthma. Marrades et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med.
research.finding: Glutathione narrowed the airways (FEV1 fell 19% versus 1% with placebo) and caused cough in 4 and breathlessness in 3 of 8 people. The authors suggested sulfite formation as the cause; a salbutamol inhaler blocked the effect.

research.summary: Double-blind crossover study of inhaled glutathione 600 mg given 30 minutes before a water-mist (fog) challenge in 12 people with mild to moderate asthma. Bagnato et al., Respiration.
research.finding: Glutathione reduced the fall in FEV1 after the fog challenge (6% versus 20% with placebo), similar to sodium cromoglycate, a standard asthma preventer.

research.summary: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial of intravenous glutathione 1,400 mg three times a week for 4 weeks in 21 people with Parkinson's disease, followed for 8 more weeks. Hauser et al., Mov Disord.
research.finding: Glutathione was well tolerated with adverse events similar to placebo. Symptom scores did not differ significantly from placebo during treatment (2.8 points better, P = 0.32) or afterward (3.5 points worse, P = 0.54).

research.summary: Review of glutathione metabolism, mechanism and evidence as a skin-lightening agent. Sonthalia, Daulatabad and Sarkar, Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol.
research.finding: Glutathione is a three-amino-acid antioxidant that keeps cells in redox balance and is proposed to lighten skin by blocking the tyrosinase enzyme and shifting melanin type. The authors found no evidence that intravenous glutathione works, noted a Philippines FDA warning against its off-label use, and said treatment duration, how long effects last and maintenance schedules remain unanswered.

research.summary: Narrative review of oral, topical and intravenous glutathione for skin lightening. Alzahrani et al., Cureus.
research.finding: Oral glutathione lowered melanin with limited side effects. The review describes a small placebo-controlled intravenous trial (Zubair et al., 1,200 mg twice weekly for 6 weeks) in which 37.5% of the treated group and 18.7% of the placebo group reported lighter skin, 32% had adverse events including liver dysfunction and one had anaphylaxis, and benefits faded over 6 months. It notes that intravenous use lacks standard dosing protocols.

dose.summary: Not approved as a drug. Studies gave 250 to 1,000 mg a day by mouth for 1 to 6 months, 1,200 to 1,400 mg by IV (intravenous, into a vein) twice or three times a week, and 600 to 646 mg by nebulizer (an inhaled mist) in small trials. Online sources describe injected doses of 100 to 600 mg and nebulized doses of 200 to 600 mg, which have not been tested in matched studies.

items.text: ScienceInsights, an educational website, says most studies of oral glutathione for skin use daily doses between 250 and 1,000 mg, and that a trial of intravenous glutathione used 1,200 mg twice weekly for six weeks. It adds that oral glutathione is limited by digestive breakdown, topical forms are used for dark spots, and IV gives the highest blood levels but carries the greatest risks.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Peptide Initiative, an educational site, lists subcutaneous (under the skin) doses of 100 mg per injection or 200 mg per injection, up to about 600 mg per week, and cites the Parkinson's IV trial dose of 1,400 mg.
items.label: internet

items.text: A compounding pharmacy site (Medivera Rx) says typical subcutaneous doses are 100 to 400 mg and intramuscular doses 200 to 600 mg, up to about 1,000 mg, and describes the product as not FDA-approved for any indication.
items.label: internet

items.text: A clinic blog (Integrative Medicine Center of Western Colorado) says to start nebulized glutathione at 1 mL (200 mg) mixed with 4 mL saline and, if tolerated, raise to 3 mL (600 mg).
items.label: internet

timing.summary: No study tested time of day. Online sources suggest mornings for oral doses, with no trial support.

items.text: The Peptide Initiative says oral glutathione is commonly taken in the morning.
items.label: internet

items.text: Plixlife, a seller of glutathione tablets, says to take glutathione in the morning 20 to 30 minutes before breakfast, or in the evening 2 to 3 hours after dinner.
items.label: internet

fasting.summary: No study tested food with glutathione. Online sources disagree: one seller says an empty stomach helps absorption, while another site says it can be taken with or without food.

items.text: Plixlife, a seller of glutathione tablets, says an empty stomach gives a clear path for absorption and to wait at least 30 minutes before eating, but also says light meals may reduce stomach upset.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Peptide Initiative says oral glutathione can be taken with or without food.
items.label: internet

frequency.summary: In studies, oral glutathione was taken daily, IV doses two or three times a week, and inhaled doses once or twice daily. Online sources describe injections one to three times a week or every 3 days and nebulizing once or twice daily. No missed-dose rules were found.

items.text: Oral doses were taken daily for 6 months in the 2015 randomized trial.

cycle_length.summary: Trials ran 4 weeks to 12 months. In people, blood levels fell back to baseline after oral glutathione stopped, and skin effects faded after IV treatment ended. Online sources say effects take 6 to 12 weeks and fade when use stops.

storage_and_handling.summary: No study covered storage. Online sellers of compounded injections say to refrigerate vials, and one site says to keep oral products cool, dry and away from light.

items.text: Medivera Rx, a compounding pharmacy, says to store glutathione injections in a refrigerator at 36 to 46 degrees F (about 2 to 8 degrees C), that the beyond-use date is about 30 days from dispensing, and that a multi-dose vial should be discarded 28 days after first puncture.
items.label: internet

items.text: Alan Health, a telehealth seller of compounded glutathione, says to keep vials refrigerated when not in use, not to freeze them, and to avoid heat and direct sunlight. It says to inject under the skin in the abdomen at least 2 inches from the belly button, the thigh or the upper arm.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Peptide Initiative says to keep oral capsules and powders in a cool, dry place away from light.
items.label: internet

mechanism.summary: Glutathione is a natural antioxidant that helps cells keep their chemical balance. It is proposed to lighten skin by blocking the enzyme tyrosinase, which is based mostly on lab data. Inhaled glutathione reached the airways in cystic fibrosis but did not change oxidative stress markers.

items.text: A review says glutathione is a tripeptide that keeps cells in redox balance and lightens skin by blocking tyrosinase and switching from dark to lighter melanin.
items.label: research

items.text: In people taking oral glutathione for 6 months, blood glutathione rose and oxidative stress markers fell, and natural killer (NK) cell activity rose at the higher level.
items.label: research

items.text: Inhaled glutathione raised glutathione in sputum but did not reduce markers of oxidative stress to proteins or fats in the airways.
items.label: research

best_documented_effect.summary: The most solid result is that oral glutathione raises blood glutathione in healthy adults. For skin lightening, a small oral and topical trial found a lower melanin index, while the single IV trial reviewed was small and its benefit faded. Trials of IV glutathione in Parkinson's disease and inhaled glutathione in cystic fibrosis found no clear benefit.

side_effect_groups.summary: Serious reactions concentrate in injected forms. In a reviewed skin trial 32% of people had adverse events including liver dysfunction and one anaphylaxis (a severe allergic reaction), though a small Parkinson's trial saw events similar to placebo.

side_effect_groups.title: Inhaled
side_effect_groups.summary: In people with mild asthma, a nebulized dose caused airway narrowing, cough and breathlessness. In cystic fibrosis trials, inhaled glutathione had side effects similar to placebo.

items.text: In 8 people with mild asthma, nebulized glutathione 600 mg cut FEV1 by 19% (placebo 1%), with cough in 4 and breathlessness in 3; salbutamol blocked the effect.
items.label: research

items.text: In another asthma study of 12 people, inhaled glutathione 600 mg reduced fog-induced airway narrowing instead.
items.label: research

items.text: In 153 people with cystic fibrosis, adverse events were similar between inhaled glutathione and placebo.
items.label: research

items.text: In 105 children and adults with cystic fibrosis, inhaled glutathione for 12 months was well tolerated.
items.label: research
